newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe tells Western critics "to go to hell".
newsitem.headline: Mugabe tells Western critics "to go to hell".

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe has told Western countries which criticised a privatisation deal his government signed in September with a Malaysian company "to go to hell".

Mugabe said he had given this message to critics of the deal under which Malaysian power producer YTL Corp Bhd would invest Z$6 billion (U.S.$568 million) in the privatisation of Hwange Thermal Power Station in northern Zimbabwe.

"There was an outcry when we decided to sign the agreement with YTL. They said there was no transparency and asked why we gave the deal to YTL. Our ambassadors were questioned by four certain western countries," he said on Sunday night at a banquet for leaders attending the Third World Group of 15 (G-15) summit.

"I told them to go to hell because Hwange thermal plant is ours and we do what we want with it. I would want to see more joint ventures among people in the south...let there be more outcries as we go into partnership with each other," he said.

The Malaysian deal drew widespread criticism from black empowerment groups, economic analysts and the former board of the state-owned Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority (ZESA), which owns Hwange, as well as some Western diplomats who queried the manner in which it was handled.

Mugabe sacked the entire ZESA board in September for opposing the deal and pressing his government to rescind a letter of intent it signed with YTL under which the Malaysian firm would control 51 percent of the equity in a joint venture company to be established for the Hwange project.
The sacked board said the agreement was contrary to the country's programme to economically empower the majority blacks and was also a departure from the government's tender system.
Before the signing of the letter of intent, ZESA had already invited bids and six foreign firms had been shortlisted, top of them a British company, while YTL was at the bottom of the list.
Last month, Mugabe said he wanted players other than Europeans to invest in his southern African country's economy.

On Sunday night, he pledged to continue cooperating with developing countries despite protests from the developed states whose main aim he said was to continue to dominate the economies of the Third World.
The three-day G-15 meeting's opening session on Sunday was dominated by speeches attacking Western countries for unfair trade practices.
